Case report. After a 3-year history of progressive stiffness of
the axial and leg muscles and painful spasms, this 30-year-old
man was diagnosed with SPS in 1990. Antibodies against glu-
tamic acid decarboxylase (antiGAD-Ab) were present in serum
(167,000 RIA [U]) and CSF (2,459 RIA [U]). Oral clonazepam,
baclofen, tizanidine, and valproic acid were not helpful. Immuno-
modulation treatment with corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, and
IV immunoglobulins achieved only temporary improvement. As
the disease progressed, the patient’s overall mobility declined con-
tinuously, and at age 35 years, he was mostly confined to a wheel-
chair. In December 1996, a programmable pump device
(Synchromed, Model 8615, Medtronic Inc., Minneapolis, MN) for
continuous ITB infusion was implanted. ITB resulted in a long-
lasting improvement, and the patient was able to walk short dis-
tances without crutches. During the first 2 years, the daily dosage
had to be gradually increased from 220 /H9262gt o6 3 2/H9262g to suppress
the spasms sufficiently. A stable period with a maintenance dos-
age of 632 /H9262g/d for some years followed. In December 2000, the
pump had to be replaced because of battery depletion. His mobil-
ity had remained stable during the past 5 years, and no substan-
tial autonomic disturbance was reported.
One day before admission, the patient developed progressive
bilateral leg spasms with a jerky onset. Spasms were elicited by
various stimuli, spread gradually to the back, abdomen, neck, and
arms, and frequently occurred in series with short pauses. Spas-
modic attacks were accompanied and often preceded by profuse
diaphoresis, hyperthermia (41 °C), arterial hypertension (210/110
mm Hg), and tachycardia (160 beats/min). Initially such attacks
lasted for up to 5 minutes, but within hours turned into an almost
continuous spasmodic storm. Repeated IV boluses of 10 mg diaze-
pam did not interrupt the spasmodic storm or the autonomic dis-
turbance. Progressive involvement of the diaphragm led to
respiratory failure; thus, mechanical ventilation was inevitable.
Despite the immediate infusion of midazolam (45 mg/h) and the
muscle relaxant atracurium (60 mg/h), the jerky spasms could not
be adequately suppressed, resulting in rhabdomyolysis with an
increase in serum creatine kinase levels (29,482 U/L). Within 1

day, his clinical condition deteriorated dramatically, and multior-
gan dysfunction developed, including arterial hypotension, cardiac
infarction and heart failure, renal failure, pneumonia, metabolic
acidosis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Meningitis
and sepsis were excluded by normal CSF analysis and repeated
blood cultures. Because continuous, severe spasms developed as
soon as the myorelaxant was reduced, failure of the ITB delivery
system was suspected.
The pump was checked to exclude an error in programming or
in the filling status of the pump or the concentration of the ba-
clofen solution (2,000 /H9262g/mL). CSF could be aspirated easily
through the side port. Biplanar radiographic films showed that
the pump and catheter were in place. Programming a bolus to
produce a rotor movement of 90° demonstrated regular rotor func-
tion, and after an injection of 5 mL radiopaque solution through
the access port, the contrast medium entered the subarachnoid
space at the tip of the catheter without any obvious leakage.
On the supposition that the pump system was working cor-
rectly, the daily ITB dosage was gradually increased from 632 /H9262g
to 1200 /H9262g; however, this did not produce any significant improve-
ment. With high doses of sedatives and myorelaxants and the full
use of intensive care treatment, including dialysis and hemofiltra-
tion (3 weeks), mechanical ventilation (5 weeks), high-dose cat-
echolamines, and substitution of various blood components, the
patient’s clinical status stabilized, and he slowly began to recover.
Continuous IV administration of midazolam was replaced by an
oral medication of 3 /H110032 mg clonazepam, but the general muscle
stiffness could not be suppressed adequately, and the attacks of
myoclonic jerks and painful spasms required repeated IV boluses
of 0.5 mg clonazepam. Thus, surgical exploration of the pump
system was planned as soon as the patient’s condition had stabi-
lized sufficiently.
Open surgery revealed a small fissure in the catheter immedi-
ately beside the connector to the pump. Leakage of the drug oc-
curred only at a definite bending of the catheter (figure).
After surgical restoration of the catheter, ITB treatment was

continued with an initial dosage of 500 /H9262g/d. Motor and autonomic
disturbances rapidly improved to the state before admission, and
the patient was discharged after a 70-day hospital stay.

The patient’s catheter was 5-years-old,
and barium-impregnated catheters may become brittle
after 5 to 10 years. Thus, surgeons should consider
replacing them at the time of pump replacement.
Malfunction of the catheter system may occur in
up to 40% of patients receiving ITB.
8 As shown in
this and other case reports, the reason may be diffi-
cult to identify
9,10 and requires a check of the whole
system according to an established protocol (table).
Our patient illustrates that noninvasive checking
methods may fail (see also reference 9). Small holes,
kinks, and fibrosis of the catheter can often only be
detected by surgery. In 20% of instances, however,
even surgery fails to identify the cause of system
malfunction, but replacing the catheter still restores
the clinical response to ITB.
